description: We are a team of students from Egypt participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge. For the "Adapting to Change" challenge, we are building a data-driven solution using NASA Earth observation data to help communities adapt to extreme weather, rising temperatures, and environmental changes. Our goal is to turn complex satellite data into simple, actionable insights that help people prepare, respond, and stay safe.
summary: During night a lot of smallholder farmers lose their crops because of heat and drought as they don’t have expensive irrigation systems. However, RootWeb is used to be free and utilize NASA satellite data to pair the farmer with native, deep-rooted "guard plants." Rather than requiring new infrastructure, these plants rely on hydraulic lift. These species shade the topsoil through the afternoon heat. At night, their deep roots draw groundwater up to keep neighboring crops alive.
details:
“What happened to my crops? Months of my backbreaking work withered into dust. How could I afford my children now? Would they starve because of me?!”. A farmer said this after finding all his crops damaged as the sun baked the topsoil dry. He looked for help everywhere, and guess what he found: only companies selling him a $5,000 automated drip-irrigation system and solar-powered IoT soil sensors. Right! because a farmer struggling to survive a drought obviously has five grand lying around for Wi-Fi-enabled sprinklers.

  RootWeb is a zero-benefit website that advises farmers to use plants with deep roots (such as Cowpea, Pigeon Pea, and Alfalfa) as biological water pumps and natural air conditioners. Using NASA satellite temperature and soil moisture indices, the platform scans any farm's thermal stress and recommends the exact intercropping pattern needed to survive climate shocks.

Hydraulic lift physics:

During daytime: The guard plant's canopy shades exposed soil between crop rows, reducing surface temperatures by up to 6.8°C and blocking water evaporation.

During nighttime: After sunset, the guard plant closes its leaf pores (stomata) to stop transpiration. Driven by water potential gradients, its deep taproots pull groundwater up from moist subsoil and release it into the dry soil, hydrating neighboring cash crops and activating soil nutrients for free. Impact: Requires $0 in hardware, reduces irrigation demand by 22% to 42%, prevents crop death during heatwaves, and naturally improves soil nitrogen.

  Moreover, the interface of the website is easy to use. All what they must do is to click on the location of their Farm on the left side, while the information like Max Temperature, Topsoil Moisture Index, Recommended Guard Plant, irrigation saved, and soil cooling is on the right. In addition, RootWeb provides a simple explanation of the physical mechanisms during the day and night in interactive photos.

  The website was coded with Python and HTML, then published on GitHub to be accessible to all farmers all around the world. Finally, the project aims to help farmers to preserve their crops without paying a lot on smart devices and to be scanned and mapped without needing a single physical device on the ground as rural areas often lack high-speed internet or field sensors. Depending on NASA’s data and the physics of nature to make an economic reality website with 0% gain.
